<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-defended cases and engaged the pressure questions directly with proper A1/A2 formatting, making this a genuinely close debate. A's asymmetric-harm framing (concentrated/irreversible recession scarring vs. diffuse/reversible inflation costs), the "tolerance with credibility, not instead of credibility" reframe, and the concrete 2022-24 disinflation-without-recession example gave it a durable evidentiary anchor that B never fully neutralized, only narrowed ("that example is exactly the case where I'd pause"). B's best move was forcing A to define a stopping point and then defining its own earlier trigger (act on stalled convergence rather than waiting for unanchoring), correctly noting policy lags cut both ways. But in the final exchange A converted this into a decisive tie-breaker: both sides concede uncertainty about their triggers, so the tie should go to the side whose error is reversible (inflation fading) rather than the side whose error is irreversible (recession scarring). B's closing restated the lag/credibility argument but did not directly rebut this reversibility tie-break, leaving A's final framing the last word standing. A's clipped opening is a real execution flaw and cost it some polish, but the missing text was largely restated later, so the substantive damage was limited.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The Pressure Questions exchange and its aftermath: A's Q1/Q2 forced B to admit uncertainty cuts both ways and to name a concrete trigger, and B's answer (tighten once inflation "stalls" rather than waiting for unanchored expectations) was a real, substantive line-drawing—but A's closing turned that same trigger back into "just another uncertain forecast," and paired it with the reversibility asymmetry that B's closing never squarely answered.</best_rebuttal>
